segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Thank you. The next speaker, please start with your name. You have three minutes. My name is Jeffrey Johnson. Serve as chair of East Tampa CRA CAC. I've been given permission to speak on our committee's behalf. The first thing is we want to address the new grants program. New construction is prohibited. Our interpretation of chapter 163 does not support that prohibition against new construction, section 163.370 provides broad redevelopment powers, including authority for construction and redevelopment activities consistent with an adopted CRP. If you look at the East Tampa CRP, it talks about several things that equates between public and private partnership. Therefore, we ask the board to add the ability for new construction under grants that are connected to the CRP. That is the document that I have submitted. Other CRAs across the State of Florida who has done new construction and how it has been funded through the CRA. So please see those exhibits. Secondly, we recommend creating a smaller exterior improvement grant, maybe up to $25,000. That does not require a property lien. Several small businesses in the community that may not own their properties cannot access the existing program because their landlords would not consent to that lien or site control. A smaller program could help tenants make basic exterior improvements while protecting the city's investment. Thirdly, we have concerns regarding the different interpretations of 163. Because the CRA relies upon one part-time attorney for legal advice, we're recommending that when a significant policy, a statutory interpretation is discussed with staff, that an elected CRA Board member participates in those conversations when legally and ethically appropriate. Currently going into FY '26, $223 million between all of our CRAs in the City of Tampa, why is there only one attorney? There should be checks and balances, and I think that would be prudent for us. Fourth, the new grant process states that the City of Tampa projects come before the CAC. That is fine. We want to make sure that those projects are a part of not being prioritized over what has already been applied for. Also, the community benefits agreement, the way we know it is being changed, we believe anything over $1 million should have public focus group to where those persons who are receiving those grants are meeting specifically with those residents and not relying just upon the CAC comments during that time. Finally, we respectfully ask the CRA Board to give substantial consideration to the recommendations of a CAC. If they give something based on recommendation of staff, whenever board extends that amount of money, we have to find where that money is going to come from in our budget and it may throw off other projects that may be down the pipeline that may not be noticed. Thank you for all you do. And those are the comments from the CAC board of East Tampa.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Start with your name. Understand quickly why so many of us are concerned. The courts are full. You'll see high school kids practicing, usta teams playing matches, people taking lessons, seniors playing with friends and kids who are just learning the game. It's an incredibly vibrant community. I don't think most people realize just how much tennis happens there. Nearly 1200 people play tennis and pickleball at hcc every week. More than 100 usta teams and pickleball teams call hcc hoping. Leagues, teams, athletes with disabilities, seniors and families who play at hcc. The special olympics and high school district tournaments are held there. Ten Tampa high schools use hcc as their home courts. They are at risk of not having a tennis season this year. So when we talk about hcc closing to make way for the new rays' stadium, we're not really talking about losing empty tennis courts. We're talking about displacing an entire sports community. The real problem is that hcc is a very large facility and there simply isn't another public tennis facility in Tampa that can reasonably absorb all of these players and programs. In fact, 26% of all tennis played in Hillsborough county happens right at hcc. In March, the rays' CEO Ken Babby said we are committed to building a world-class tennis center as part of this project. He talked about Al Lopez Park as a potential site. When I heard that, I thought this is great. Let's make the commitment a reality. We're getting a new major league baseball stadium. We're making an enormous investment in Tampa. Why not use this opportunity to create something our entire community can be proud of? Imagine a beautiful public tennis and pickleball center with clay courts, hard courts and covered courts, a facility that can accommodate the people who already play at hcc, but is also good enough to bring larger tournaments and events to Tampa. A place where a child can pick up a racket for the first time without having to belong to a private club. My name is pippin gilbert. I'm a Tampa native, a Hillsborough county resident, and an avid tennis player. I'm also a rays' fan. I'm not asking anyone to stop progress. I'm asking us to plan for it. Please keep hcc tennis open through April so our school teams can finish their seasons. Before these courts are demolished, let's have a real replacement plan with a location, enough courts, funding and construction timeline. We have an opportunity to do something impactful. Let's keep tennis and pickleball part of our thriving Tampa community. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Thank you. Next speaker, please start with your name. You'll have three minutes. My name is Bishop Michelle b. Patty. I would like to start off by thanking carolyn collins and her committee for all the outstanding hard work they have put into the Jackson house. Been a lifelong resident 73 years to be exact. I've watched segregation into integration. There's not a lot of things that isn't in the City of Tampa that still show where african americans, where we were segregated and most of these places now, there are monuments, little stickers, and some of them not even in the right place. I attended dobyville elementary school. The marker is not where the original dobyville elementary school was at. And so I don't want the Jackson house to become a place such as that. In 199 -- 1905, a gentleman by the name of santiago. He coined a phrase, he say those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it. So what we're saying with the Jackson house, it's not just a run-down building, a building that is dilapidated. It has rich black history. This committee has worked long and hard. I watched them overcome roadblock after roadblock. I remember Mr. Robinson coming to this council time and time again to get this done and it fell on deaf ears. Now the committee has picked the ball up. A lot of things from easement to applications to -- that has been a stumbling block. I stood before the same council and supported the rays coming here, and you all have not hesitated to give millions and millions of dollars to this sports complex. What african americans, we are taxpayers, that we're asking that we continue the project. Yes, I know that there were parts of it that have fallen in. But they have a plan. The plan, we should stick to it, but we should hastily, hastily help them implement it so that all can be reserved and saved. I remember vividly as a young woman, young girl, rather, walking from Hyde Park to downtown Tampa only to have to go into the bottom of kress and wool-worth because we were not allowed to sit at the counter. We could not go in the front of the store. Many of you are too young to know that existed. Racism did exist. It's alive and well today. He want to preserve the history, the last history we have left. Hyde Park that I knew is gone. Central park, all these places has been eroded. Now the Jackson house represent a whole lot more than what people are giving it credit for. I'm asking this council to do your due diligence and look at the rich history we have and preserve it, please. Thank you.

Williams who was one of the charter members of the kappa chapter here in Tampa. Kappa league members, some of the kappa league members were a part of the program. We talked about fanny b. Stone, who was a mortician over the stone funeral home. We also talked about inez boyer who started the helping hands nursery day care. So the kids were able to learn about them, and they got fed, and they got to walk around. They went on a walking tour. They enjoyed that. I'm trying to get through this so that way I do my due diligence of saying thank you. I really appreciate everybody's help with this program. Moving forward. My battery is about to die. Development, chairman mcknight on being told that the council was ready to hear anything he might have to say stated that he had come with other colored men from the section of the city known as the scrub, but properly defined as east and southeast Tampa. Southeast Tampa being the garrison. People wanted new streetlights, one or two lights and main from the water works. He was informed by chairman that he would have to make his request in writing, which he did, retiring for that purpose in a few minutes, he reappeared with a written one embodying substantially what he previously said. He was instructed to tell constituents to rest assured that they would receive lights, water and streets would be open at the earliest practical time. The petition was referred to proper committees with instruction to give these matters their immediate attention. Now, when we go further in the newspaper articles, it took a few years for all of this to get done. The community, obviously, came out wanting basic things -- water and lights. In East Tampa, we want new construction. We want things that are going to generate and attract developers to our area. So we need new construction in our area. I would really appreciate if you guys would consider that rule being changed, if it's already written, unwrite it and make it so we can have an easier path to new development in East Tampa. Thank you all.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: Next speaker, start with your name. You have three minutes. Connie burton. The history of black people in this city usually start with once upon a time. Once upon a time, that existed over there. Once upon a time there was a vibrant Central Avenue where black folks were able to take care of their basic needs. 34th street, 29th street all was once upon a time. So that's why I thought and the former councilperson thought resolution 568 was important. It was important not just because it would identify the past harm but it was a pathway to move forward. Seems to me you need a guide map to move forward. It's very unfortunate and hard-breaking to see how certain developers can come here and immediately all of their work go to the top of the chain, immediately, because you think it will bring some court of revenue to the city, and it might. But what we see in our community is of such value, but still dealing with once upon a time because we're not able to get the type of development that we want. We're not able to restore the things that we want. When we look inside at the african community, the reality is we got high unemployment. We've got health disparity. We need real affordable housing for working-class people. I'm always talking about East Tampa because that's where I reside. I know that people in East Tampa do not make a hundred thousand dollars. They might want to, but that's not the reality. I know in East Tampa, there is a high drop-out rate. I know that in East Tampa many of the buildings that exist in East Tampa now has been there -- I'm 70, so they got to be at least 150 years old because they was there when I was a child and my mother was a child. What has this council or what is this city prepared to do to bring on new development? You got to have the courage to do it. You got to say the investment we need cannot be based on once upon a time or one pot of gold and I'm looking at now what fair oaks is, and then people will rest their laurels they have done all they can for East Tampa. There is a lot of work that needs to be done in our community. Our community, our young people should be able to see the value in african investment from their parents and as we move forward, they can see new development is still emerging inside of a seamless city, inside of a seamless city that is welcoming to all. The statute limits to you repair and rehabilitation of existing structures. I walked through the 500-year-old downtown and went to the museum, between the nazis and soviets they destroyed the entire thing. Warsaw went back to paintings from the 1700s and rebuilt their entire old town. I saw a video the other day on a town in Germany that did the same thing. Williamsburg, most people don't realize that 90% of the buildings there were rebuilt in the '20s. Now they are a hundred years old, but they are not from the 1700s. Some of them, but not all of them. St. augustine, because it was burned down twice, there are no buildings except a stone building from the 1600s. And a lot of the buildings that look old are new. So the point is -- manhattan casino we mentioned in st. pete was a very popular, important building in the African American community, was rebuilt. We can rebuild it. If it falls down, we rebuild it. My question is to maybe the new contractors, as I understand it, the process is called appeal -- called a peel where you take it apart and mark each -- like a construction site, could be a pyramid or old building, take it apart and mark each piece of wood, where it goes. You already have the laser scan. We have photographs. Is that still the process? When is the peel going to start? If we did the peel right away and nothing there, that would be better than watching chunks of it fall. Next question, if we can only use 15%, will that meet the state or federal guidelines on historic preservation? For the last part of your question, the latter -- Angela Scott. The only requirement for the -- not the only, but one of the requirements for the historic preservation is for, as Dr. Collins stated earlier, we need to make sure that the exterior of this home is built just like the time period of 1950 to 1959. That is the goal and that's what the architect and that's what we're working with the historic preservation office here locally and on statewide to make sure that that takes place. It's not a percentage of wood or anything of that nature. We work with the preservation office to make sure we get the right material as Mr. Ronnie Williams indicated earlier for the latter part of your question.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you, madam chair. I appreciate that. You know, it's funny, when we saw the news about what happened a few days ago with the Jackson house, it's symbolic to people in the sense that it's falling apart. Obviously, people know that in reconstruction, you'll have to do radical measures on the house, obviously, but just the falling apart is obviously problematic. Like Councilman Carlson said, I've seen on social media some comments on people that say that the city should have no business in this and even saying some people. Social media, all it takes is a couple of hands and time to write down something and send it. I've seen people go that it should be torn down, this and that. For me, if somebody has such gross disrespect for our black history and for african americans and our american history dealing with black americans, they can go to hell. That's it. That's just the way that it is. Amen. I cursed. There you go. It's true. For me, that's terrible. It's funny. We look at other communities. I went out to Mississippi a year ago. Great u.s. history nerd, I guess. I went out to money, Mississippi. I saw the barn where emmett till was murdered and also saw Bryant's grocery store where emmitt was sold to Ms. Bryant. If you look at the store, it's in terrible condition. The son of a juror who acquitted emmett till's murderers owns that store, that building and refuses it to sell it to the state of Mississippi for less than $5 million. We can look at that and judge that and say that's terrible, that's terrible. But we got the Jackson house. There are legal procedural issues that precluded us from going forward, but that's something that is a challenge to us here in Tampa in terms of honoring that history. And thank god we can go forward now. That's the great thing. Now, why is it important for us to honor that? The Jackson house is one of many parts of the City of Tampa where there is a brutal, violent, ugly Jim Crow era history from the end of reconstruction until 1930s. It was the State of Florida that had the highest per capita rate of lynchings in the United States of America. City of Tampa was not immune. Just outside of city hall part of a lynching, Robert Johnson, 1934, a transfer from police officers I think from the county to the city, just outside of city hall down to Ybor City, Louis Jackson was lynched in 1903 I think it was. Incident after incident of that. Jim Crow, and Jim Crow, as folks know, wasn't just as terrible as it is. Separate restrooms or separate accommodations, as terrible as that is, it was violence and lynching such that 6 million african americans over about a 50-year period fled the south to up north in a great migration. You take a look at that, that's what the Jackson house is all about, which is a small microcosm of paying tribute to that suffering so that we don't forget our history, especially in the year 2026 or whenever you talk about this stuff, you have folks who are obsessed with grievance and ultraridiculous sensitivity on issues. Oh, we don't want to hear about that. We ought to tell it from the rooftop because that's how we got here. A good country makes wrongs right. We repair breaches, and that's what we should be doing. And also agree with something that Councilman Carlson said with regards to Councilwoman Young, which is I would be interested in seeing what you think are the next steps, not to put pressure on you, as you are the person leading the charge over here, I pay you kind deference. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: Okay. So you're going to disassemble. You're going to re-create and restore. Some people will say, well, it's not the Jackson. It's not original. I want you to google 1954 ferrari mondial. It's a car sold at auction for $1.9 million. It looks like a crash vehicle that you would think it's scrap metal. Going to cost $2 million to restore it. Send it to the factory and it's going to be certified by the company because the company, and you are probably wondering what does this have to do with the Jackson house. Ferrari has the blueprints to all the cars they have manufactured, just like you have 3d scans and the blueprints for the Jackson house. Some will argue it's not the original ferrari that raced in the 1950s. Once it is done, it will be worth, I don't know, 10, $20 million. I don't know. Once the Jackson house is done, it's not about the monetary value, it's about this is how things are restored. There's also a story about a Mercedes rotting in Cuba for years. 1.5, 2 million dollars. Rotting under a tree and it was restored and on the road again. It's worth a fortune. The Jackson house applies to that. People are disassembling and re-creating and restoring, it's going to be the Jackson house. It's going to be a Jackson house that's going to withstand the test of time and be there for multiple generations to come, just like these cars that are going to be worth -- that are worth money, but are going to be worth even more once they are done. It's the same thing with this. What you can't replace historically, this is the Jackson house. This will continue to be the Jackson house, and this is how things are often restored. When people drive by and see, oh, it will fall over, in a strong wind, we have to, as was mentioned earlier, we have to understand, it's going to be taken apart carefully. We're going to go piece by piece. We're going to repurpose for artwork, for other reasons, and then we're going to restore and salvage what we can and then the Jackson house will rise again and be there for years to come. Thank you.

segments.text: Yeah, again, I think it would be helpful for your new team to come together sooner rather than later. The story doesn't die and the story doesn't get blown down by a hurricane. The important thing here is retaining the story. So I think if you were to do a one-pager and say, this is what we're doing. This is our objective. Our objective is to retain that story. It's to rebuild that structure so we have a place to tell the story and that we clearly communicate that, again, I think it will alleviate a lot of the anxiety people have every time the wind blows. segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I think again with the common language that we all understand what the process is moving forward that we're not under the misunderstanding that we're trying to retain 80% of this building in its original. We took the original house, all of the rooms, upstairs and down stairs, we gave it to the board, because we had already been to the community. The community had been telling us what they wanted to see. The way we tell that story, you are absolutely right. Because the story is not just a house. It's that family as well that stayed in the house and had economic development before it was popular. It's not just the african americans that were fortunate to stay there, but the native americans, the military families and all that contribute to other parts of Tampa, that was also able to stay there. Yes, that's exactly what we're trying to do. And we're asking people when we go to those quarterly meetings what you want to see, what you want to do. I can even remember Councilman Carlson told us, even about pictures that he had. We've talked about judges who want to redo different products and retrofit them or resurface or whatever. segments.text: Thank you. One, I want to thank everybody for their comments. Since that CRA meeting, we have spoken a lot, probably multiple times a day. You have to have the exact same dimensions for the windows. Exact same dimensions for the doors. Everything has to be very much -- it's very technical. We talked about that. We went all the way back to when the project first started. You gave me the history down to the easements and alleys. We had a full discussion just so I can kind of get the background of this project. So we need to be SMART, not just benefit certain people's clients, because they want to develop in that area. We had a proposal to put it through the middle, so to bisect the compromise, which everybody agreed to, was to put it between the aquarium parking lot and the cruise terminals and go north, the port building is in the way so we'd have to figure out how to go around that. We'll report it to the proper authorities because it's not acceptable to treat staff like that. Especially when we're trying to do something good for the community. segments.text: Yes, sir. What that means, very briefly, is when we provide a grant for a project of whatever type --

segments.speaker: Cliff Shepard
segments.text: Essentially, whatever project we're doing, whether it's commercial or residential, it should have in it our expectations for what we're getting for our money. Someone mentioned earlier, for example, painting and fixing up. And that might be the expectation. Those grants are supposed to be reimbursements. Theoretically, we get the grant money -- we give the grant money after that's done. Let's suppose, for example. This has not happened but actually happened that one of the places fixed up with grant money is then unexpectedly sold to, I don't know, a motorcycle club, like maybe the outlaws. I'm just saying from experience, and then it gets painted black with razor wire fence put around it and we have CRA money in it. So the idea of the lien is over the covenants, if they violate the covenants by not keeping it in whatever condition we want it in for whatever period of time, I think typically we say five years, depends what it is. Affordable housing, obviously longer and so forth. We have the ability to get the money back. It's a violation of the covenants. Usually the covenants have a descending scale. Within the first year, we get all the money back. If in year two, it's -- we get 80% and so forth. Descends down to zero after year five. For the smaller grants that we're talking about. Obviously, other grants have different time periods based on what we're trying to get. I think the affordable housing may go up to 50 years.
